facts.claim: Two meta-analyses on the effect, which focused on generosity measured by donations and economic games, suggest that artificial surveillance cues do not influence the donation amount.
facts.quote: Two meta-analyses on the effect, which focused on generosity measured by donations and economic games, suggest that artificial surveillance cues do not influence the donation amount.

facts.claim: Women give more than men in South America, North America and Oceania, while they give less than men in South Africa.
facts.quote: On the other hand, women give more than men in South America, North America and Oceania, while they give less than men in South Africa.

facts.claim: A meta-analysis of 15 experiments involving 2035 participants shows that photographs and/or stylized images of eyes reduced antisocial behaviour by 35%.
facts.quote: Our meta-analysis of 15 experiments involving 2035 participants shows that photographs and/or stylized images of eyes reduced antisocial behaviour by 35%.

facts.claim: Women are on average significantly more generous than men, even if controlling for several moderator variables that are included in the study.
facts.quote: It is found that gender differences exist, being women on average significantly more generous than men, even if controlling for several moderator variables that are included in the study.

research.angle: While some meta-analyses show that eye cues reduce antisocial behavior, other meta-analyses suggest these cues do not influence donation amounts.
research.verdict: The evidence is contradictory, showing that eye cues may reduce antisocial behavior but do not necessarily increase generosity in donation-based settings.
research.caveat: The number of people around when a donation decision is made is identified as a potentially important factor that can bias results.
